content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler Biscuit is a gentle dry baked snack specially formulated for children aged 6 months to 3 years. It is made from whole grains, contains no added sugar or artificial flavors, making it safe and easy to digest.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Produced using low‑temperature baking to preserve maximum nutrients.
Contains whole oat flakes, rice flour and a small amount of fruit puree for natural sweetness.
Gluten‑free, suitable for children with gluten sensitivity.
One serving (30 g) provides about 120 kcal, convenient for portion control.
The biscuit dissolves easily in the mouth, reducing choking risk for young kids.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Whole grains deliver sustained energy and help maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2 and B6 support nervous system development and metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron is essential for hemoglobin formation and helps prevent anemia in children.

items.title: Natural antioxidants
items.content: Fruit puree (e.g., apple) provides vitamin C and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: A modest amount of dietary fiber promotes a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Grain allergy
items.content: Children with known allergies to wheat, rice or oats should consult a pediatrician before introducing the product.

items.title: Portion control
items.content: Excessive consumption may lead to unwanted weight gain due to the biscuit’s caloric content.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Despite its soft texture, infants under 12 months should be offered the biscuit under supervision.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The biscuit can be served as a standalone snack, softened in milk, baby juice or water. It also works well mixed into porridge, yogurt or fruit puree for added variety.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in the original packaging in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, reseal tightly or transfer to an airtight container. Shelf life: 12 months.

bread-wheat-or-cracked-wheat-made-from-h.title: Bread, wheat or cracked wheat, homemade or bakery purchase

content.title: About
content.content: Bread made from wheat or cracked wheat is a baked product prepared from whole grain wheat, whole‑grain flour or coarsely ground wheat. It can be homemade or bought from a bakery. The loaf features a distinctive aroma, a dense crumb and a lightly crisp crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wheat is one of the oldest cultivated crops, grown for more than 10,000 years.
Cracked wheat retains most of the bran and germ, boosting the nutritional value of the bread.
Homemade bread often undergoes a longer fermentation, enhancing flavor and aroma.
Traditional bakeries frequently use sourdough starter instead of commercial yeast for better taste and digestibility.
Whole‑wheat bread contains more fiber, B‑vitamins and minerals than white bread.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain bread provides soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting gut health and promoting satiety.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Wheat delivers slow‑releasing glucose, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, niacin and folate in whole‑grain bread aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Magnesium, iron and zinc contribute to muscle function, blood formation and immune health.

items.title: Probiotic effect of sourdough
items.content: Sourdough bread contains lactic‑acid bacteria that may improve intestinal microbiota.

items.title: Wheat allergy or gluten intolerance
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions or gluten sensitivity, leading to digestive discomfort.

items.title: High glycemic index of white bread
items.content: Bread made from refined flour can cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes, which is undesirable for diabetics.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Certain breads contain significant amounts of salt; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium options.

items.title: Mold and mycotoxins
items.content: Improper storage can lead to mold growth, producing toxins harmful to health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bread can be eaten plain, used for sandwiches, served with soups, made into toast, croutons or breadcrumbs. For extra flavor, toast slices and add olive oil, avocado or a spread of your choice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep bread in a paper bag or bread box at room temperature for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag and thaw in a toaster or oven. Avoid moisture to prevent mold growth.

egg-substitute-omelet-scrambled-or-fried.title: Egg substitute, omelet, scrambled, or fried with cheese and meat

content.title: About
content.content: Egg substitute is a ready‑made blend that allows you to make an omelet, scrambled eggs or fried dish without using real eggs. The formula typically contains plant proteins, starch, flavorings and sometimes additives that mimic the taste and texture of eggs. Cheese and meat can be added for a hearty, protein‑rich meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Egg substitute is a staple in vegan cooking because it is completely plant‑based.
Many blends include nutritional yeast, which gives a characteristic "egg‑like" aroma.
Some brands fortify the product with vitamins B12 and D, nutrients usually found in eggs.
When cooked correctly, the substitute achieves the same fluffiness as a traditional omelet.
It is shelf‑stable and usually sold dry, so no refrigeration is needed before opening.

items.title: Low cholesterol
items.content: Unlike real eggs, the substitute contains no cholesterol, which is beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: The blend provides a complete amino‑acid profile to support muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Fortified versions supply B12, B2 and folate, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Starch and added fiber help maintain regular bowel function.

items.title: Culinary versatility
items.content: Easily combined with cheese, meat, or vegetables for a wide range of flavors.

items.title: Soy or pea protein allergy
items.content: Many substitutes are based on soy or pea protein, which can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared mixes often contain added salt; choose low‑sodium options if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Missing micronutrients
items.content: Compared with eggs, the substitute may lack lutein and choline in sufficient amounts.

items.title: Processed ingredients
items.content: Some brands use artificial flavors and preservatives.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Combine the dry mix with water (or plant milk) in the recommended ratio, whisk to a smooth batter and cook in a lightly oiled pan like a regular omelet. Add grated cheese and diced meat a few minutes before the dish is done so they melt and heat through.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dry egg substitute in a sealed container in a cool, dry place. After opening, use within 6–12 months. Cooked batter should be kept refrigerated and consumed within 24 hours.

fruit-flavored-drink-with-high-vitamin-c.title: Fruit Flavored Drink Powder with High Vitamin C

content.title: About
content.content: The fruit flavored drink powder with high vitamin C is designed for quick preparation of a refreshing beverage. The powder does not require pre‑mixing and can be added directly to water or another liquid. Its taste resembles a blend of citrus and berries, and the high vitamin C content makes it a beneficial addition to the diet.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The powdered format allows long‑term storage without loss of flavor.
Vitamin C is stabilized to retain its properties even after extended shelf life.
The product contains no sugar, but can be sweetened according to personal preference.
It is often used by athletes and travelers as a fast source of vitamins.
The powder is easy to transport, does not spill, and does not require refrigeration.

items.title: High vitamin C content
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system, aids collagen synthesis, and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Hydration support
items.content: Adding the powder to water makes it more palatable, encouraging fluid intake.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Vitamin C participates in iron metabolism and helps convert food into energy.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Antioxidants protect cells from oxidative stress, which is especially important during physical activity.

items.title: Convenient usage
items.content: The powder is easy to dose, allowing precise control of vitamin intake.

items.title: Allergy to fruit flavorings
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to the flavoring components.

items.title: Excessive vitamin C intake
items.content: Very high doses of vitamin C can cause gastrointestinal discomfort.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Vitamin C may affect the efficacy of certain drugs, such as anticoagulants.

items.title: Not suitable for young children
items.content: Due to the high concentration of vitamin C, dosage for children should be monitored.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add one‑two servings (as indicated on the package) of powder to a glass of cold water, stir thoroughly until fully dissolved. Optionally, add ice, mint, or a splash of juice to enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the packet in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the package tightly sealed to prevent moisture ingress.

content.title: About
content.content: The pomegranate beverage contains 40‑50 % pomegranate juice and belongs to the light non‑alcoholic drink category. It offers a bright fruity flavor with a mildly sweet‑tart aftertaste and lower calories compared to pure juice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pomegranate juice is rich in polyphenols, especially anthocyanins, which give the drink its deep red color.
The sugar content is lower than in 100 % juice because the juice is diluted with water.
Pomegranate has been used traditionally in Mediterranean cuisine and is a symbol of abundance and health.
In many markets, drinks with 40‑50 % juice are labeled “light,” indicating reduced calories and sugar.
Pomegranate trees can live over 200 years, with harvests typically from September to November.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Polyphenols in pomegranate juice help neutralize free radicals and support cellular health.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Studies suggest regular consumption may help lower blood pressure and improve lipid profiles.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Acids and dietary fiber in the juice stimulate gastrointestinal function.

items.title: Immune system boost
items.content: Vitamin C and other phytochemicals contribute to stronger immune defenses.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: Dilution with water makes the beverage less calorie‑dense, suitable for weight management.

items.title: Pomegranate allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to pomegranate.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although labeled “light,” people with diabetes should still monitor overall glycemic impact.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Pomegranate can affect the metabolism of certain drugs, such as statins; consult a physician if you take medication.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Serve chilled as a refreshing snack, use in cocktails, smoothies, or as a base for fruit punches. It pairs well with mint, lime, and berries.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 5‑7 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Pig's feet are the meat and gelatin obtained from the lower limbs of a pig. They are rich in collagen, have a deep meaty flavor, and develop a slightly jelly‑like texture after long cooking. They are commonly used in stocks, stews, braised dishes, and as appetizers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pig's feet contain a large amount of gelatin that turns into a rich broth when simmered slowly.
In many traditional cuisines (e.g., Russian, Polish, Chinese) pig's feet are considered a delicacy and feature in festive meals.
Collagen from pig's feet is often processed into food‑grade gelatin used in jellies and desserts.
When cooked properly, the meat becomes tender enough to melt in the mouth.
Pig's feet are frequently served cold after marinating in vinegar and spices.

items.title: Rich in collagen
items.content: Collagen supports skin elasticity, joint health, and connective‑tissue repair.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: Provides high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and tissue maintenance.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Contains iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for blood health, immunity, and bone strength.

items.title: Glucosamine and chondroitin
items.content: These compounds, present in the cartilage of the feet, may aid joint function.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Suitable for low‑carb diets when prepared without added sugars.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Pig's feet can be fatty, so people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Potential pathogens
items.content: Improper cooking may leave bacteria such as Salmonella; thorough heat treatment is required.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pork.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Those prone to gout should limit intake due to purines.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Feet are usually boiled or braised for several hours until tender, used in stocks, soups, stews, or marinated in vinegar with spices. After pre‑cooking they can be roasted in the oven to develop a crispy crust.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh pig's feet in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Before cooking, inspect for off‑odors or discoloration and discard if present.

content.title: About
content.content: Soft pretzels are ready‑to‑eat snack twists made from wheat flour, water, yeast and a pinch of salt. After baking they are brushed with melted butter and lightly sprinkled with sea salt, giving them a distinctive aroma and flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pretzels have a medieval origin in Europe and were originally baked by monks.
The twisted shape is said to represent “interlaced arms,” a symbol of friendship and hospitality.
Soft pretzels are a classic accompaniment to beer in German and Austrian pubs.
Butter coating adds richness but also increases the calorie count.
In the 19th century they became a popular street food in the United States, especially in New York City.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Pretzels provide a quick source of energy thanks to the complex carbs in the wheat dough.

items.title: Contains some protein
items.content: Wheat flour supplies a modest amount of plant‑based protein useful for tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin content
items.content: Yeast‑leavened dough retains B1, B2 and niacin, which support metabolic processes.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Salt and a small amount of iron contribute to electrolyte balance.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: Butter and salt enhance flavor, helping to satisfy cravings and potentially reduce consumption of sweeter snacks.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Excessive intake of salted pretzels may contribute to elevated blood pressure.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Butter coating and carbs make the product energy‑dense; portion control is advisable.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Pretzels contain wheat, so they are unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: The butter topping can trigger reactions in individuals allergic to milk proteins.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pretzels can be enjoyed straight from the pack, warmed in a microwave or oven, and used as a base for sandwiches with cream cheese, hummus, or jam.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed package in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life store in the refrigerator to prevent drying out and butter spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Saccharin is an artificial sweetener about 300–400 times sweeter than sugar but contains no calories. The liquid form is convenient for adding to drinks, sauces, baked goods and confectionery. It is heat‑stable and has a long shelf life.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Saccharin was discovered in 1879 by German chemist Constantin F. Fahlberg.
Originally it was used medically as a cough suppressant and for diabetes treatment.
In the 1970s the United States imposed a temporary ban on saccharin over cancer concerns, but later studies lifted the restriction.
Liquid saccharin is widely used in soft drinks and energy beverages.
Saccharin does not affect blood glucose levels, making it suitable for diabetic products.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: Saccharin provides sweetness without adding calories, helping with weight‑management diets.

items.title: Does not raise blood sugar
items.content: The sweetener has a zero glycemic index, making it safe for people with diabetes.

items.title: Heat stability
items.content: Saccharin retains its sweetness during cooking and baking, useful for a wide range of recipes.

items.title: Bitter aftertaste
items.content: At high concentrations saccharin can leave a characteristic bitter aftertaste.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergy symptoms such as itching, rash or swelling.

items.title: Children’s intake
items.content: Because it may influence taste preferences, saccharin consumption should be limited for young children.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add 1–2 drops of liquid saccharin per 100 ml of beverage, sauce, marinade or batter. In baking it replaces sugar at a ratio of about 1 : 300–400 (by sweetness).

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a tightly sealed bottle in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For long‑term storage check for sediment or off‑odors before use.

content.title: About
content.content: Sweet potato fries are thin strips of sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) that are cooked until crisp. Sweet potatoes are cultivated in warm climates, have a naturally sweet flavor, bright orange flesh, and are rich in beta‑carotene.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sweet potatoes belong to the morning‑glory family, not to the true potato family.
They contain two‑to‑three times more vitamin A than regular potatoes.
Sweet potatoes were domesticated in South America over 5,000 years ago.
Proper frying retains most of the fiber and antioxidants.
In many countries sweet potato fries are a staple in school cafeterias.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene converts to vitamin A in the body, supporting vision, immunity, and skin health.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Good source of potassium
items.content: Potassium supports heart function, muscle contraction, and fluid balance.

items.title: Lower glycemic impact when baked
items.content: Baking or air‑frying sweet potatoes results in a lower glycemic index compared with regular potatoes.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Anthocyanins and vitamin C protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High carbohydrate content
items.content: Large portions can raise blood glucose, which is important for people with diabetes.

items.title: Oil frying
items.content: Deep‑frying in excess oil adds calories and may introduce trans fats if the wrong oil is used.

items.title: Nightshade allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to sweet potatoes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve sweet potato fries hot, seasoned with salt, spices, or herbs. They can be baked, air‑fried, or deep‑fried and pair well with yogurt‑based dips, guacamole, or classic ketchup.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cooked fries keep in the refrigerator in an airtight container for 2‑3 days. Raw sweet potato sticks should be stored in a cool, dry place, and for longer storage kept refrigerated wrapped in plastic.
